idea.value: Social posting across many networks stops being six separate chores and becomes one sentence typed to an AI assistant: ask in a chat, wait one beat, see the finished work.

audience.value: People who already use an AI chat assistant and run social accounts for a small business or brand: the worked example is a small bakery announcing a product across six networks, the copy speaks of a whole week planned, and every action is a chat request rather than a dashboard workflow.
evidence: speech-text.json bakery handle and calendar header at 13.017 s and 22.017 s
speech-text.json chat requests at 5.017-7.517 s, 17.517-19.017 s, 27.517 s

value.device: Problem shown as a grid of failures, without words: six composer cards each collect a different warning chip while a cursor hops between them, ending with every card outlined in red or amber.
value.description: 0.00-0.30 s: six dark cards appear in a 3x2 grid. 0.3-3.5 s: a cursor visits card after card, draft lines fill them and a red or amber warning chip lands under each, roughly every half second, under a slow 14% push-in. 3.50-3.67 s: all six outlines glow red or amber; hard cut to a light frame. The viewer recognises the chore (each network wants something different) before any product or claim, so the first title answers a felt problem.

value.retentionDevice: recognisable frustration that escalates card by card
value.content: Six channel composer cards, each failing with its own warning chip.

value.retentionDevice: a request typing in real time, then an instant confident reply
value.content: Serif positioning line on cream; a chat bubble asks to schedule a launch everywhere at a set time; reply bubble confirms six channels, six versions.

value.retentionDevice: one-bar dark loader with a looping mark
value.content: Partner mark animates, status label says posts are being drafted.

value.purpose: Proof one: one input, many tailored outputs
value.content: A source post card, a two-line caption, then six channel-specific posts fan out with check chips and a scheduled toast.

value.retentionDevice: relatable time promise plus a bigger request
value.content: Two-line serif benefit about a week planned in minutes; a chat bubble asks for the remaining days to be scheduled at the best times.

value.retentionDevice: the now-familiar loader signals another result
value.content: Same loader, label about finding the best times.

value.retentionDevice: events landing one by one, a climbing counter, then a pull-back to the whole week
value.content: A week calendar fills with channel-coloured events placed by the assistant's cursor; the view pulls back to the complete board.

value.retentionDevice: no loader this time; the answer arrives within 2 s
value.content: Dark chat: a request to publish one post now; the reply says it is live, with three live status chips.

value.retentionDevice: the verb of a held line is edited live, twice
value.content: One line naming three verbs in turn (the three asks) and the one place they all happen.

value.retentionDevice: logo pop with overshoot, tagline, fade to black
value.content: Mark and wordmark, tagline repeating the category line, and the web address.

payoff.value: The full week board pulled back into view (25.0-25.5 s) and the instant 'it is live' reply (29.6 s): the chores from the hook are done by three sentences.

callToAction.value: Soft: the end card shows the mark, the category tagline and the web address for 3 s; no button or spoken instruction.

whyItWorks: The hook shows the pain as a picture (six cards, six different warnings) so the first title answers something the viewer already feels.

A fixed three-step loop (ask on a light card, one-bar dark loader, result on a light interface) is learned on the first pass and recognised on the second, so the second and third asks cost no attention to read.
Each proof escalates scope: one post into six, one post into a whole week, then publishing immediately with no wait at all.
Every request is a short human sentence in a chat bubble and every answer is visible work, which makes the claim (do it from the chat) demonstrated rather than stated.
The summary line edits its own verb with a named cursor, so the closing claim is acted out by the product's own gesture.
Shot lengths of 4, 8 or 12 beats and cuts placed a couple of frames ahead of the kick make a dense 40 s feel calm and metred (inferred from measured timing; the soundtrack was not heard).
